passages.happening:
“The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth: Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers” (verses 1-2).

“For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
This is a personal letter, the most personal of John's three. The elder writes to one friend, Gaius, and he calls him ‘beloved’ again and again.

We know nothing of Gaius beyond this letter. Gaius was one of the most common Roman names, and the New Testament mentions several men called Gaius, but there is no good reason to think this is any of them. What the letter shows is enough: he was loved, he was faithful, and he was generous.

The elder's opening wish follows the custom of the time. Surviving papyrus letters regularly begin with a prayer or wish for the reader's health, much as we might write, ‘I hope you are well’. The elder prays that Gaius will ‘prosper and enjoy good health’, body and soul alike. The word for prosper first meant to have a good road, and so to go well. The elder is not talking about money.

Then comes his joy. Travelling Christians had come back with news: Gaius was walking in the truth. ‘I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.’ ‘My children’ may mean people the elder had brought to faith, or simply believers in his care. Either way, his greatest joy is not success or numbers. It is people living what they believe.
passages.ot:
A prayer for a friend's good is as old as Israel. Jonathan and David pledged their friendship before the LORD (1 Samuel 20:42).

The psalm pictures the person rooted in God's word as a tree: “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither, and who prospers in all he does” (Psalm 1:3). That is a picture of a life bearing fruit, not a promise of riches.

And the wisdom books link a right life with health in a general way: “Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil. This will bring healing to your body and refreshment to your bones” (Proverbs 3:7-8). Proverbs describes how life usually goes, not a guarantee for every case.
passages.hard:
Does verse 2 promise that faithful Christians will be wealthy and healthy?

No. Read in its setting, it is a friend's greeting and prayer, in the custom of letters of the time. It is a prayer for one man, not a promise to every Christian. The word translated ‘prosper’ first meant to have a good road, to go well; it is not a word about money.

Yet the verse has often been used to teach that God wills wealth and health for every believer who has enough faith, or who gives enough. This is often called prosperity teaching, or the prosperity gospel. It is one of the things this site does not teach as true. Many who teach it are sincere, and many who believe it are hoping for help in hard times. They deserve care, not scorn. But it is a mistake, and this verse does not support it. The New Testament shows faithful believers who were poor, sick and persecuted, and Jesus warned against the love of wealth.

What the verse does show is that it is right to pray for another person's body and daily needs as well as their soul. God cares about the whole person.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whom you could pray for today, body and soul. Ask what gives you your greatest joy, and whether it is people walking in the truth. And ask whether you have believed, or been told, that illness or poverty means your faith was weak.

passages.happening:
“Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you. They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God” (verses 5-6).

“For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
Gaius had welcomed travelling Christian workers, ‘brothers’, though he did not know them. In the Roman world travel was common but costly and risky. Inns had a poor name, and travellers depended on networks of family, friends and patrons. Early Christians built such a network out of their churches.

‘Send them on their way’ was almost a set phrase for this. It meant giving food, money and perhaps company for the next stage of the trip. Paul asks the same of churches for himself and his helpers (Romans 15:24; Titus 3:13). The elder asks Gaius to do it ‘in a manner worthy of God’, as if he were sending God's own messengers.

Why? Because ‘they went out on behalf of the Name’, the name of Jesus. And they were ‘accepting nothing from the Gentiles’: they did not take support from unbelievers. Many wandering teachers and philosophers of the time lived on public gifts and were suspected of preaching for profit. These workers would not. That meant someone in the church had to support them.

‘Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.’ The word ‘fellow workers’ is the one Paul uses for his co-workers. Gaius did not travel. But by opening his home he shared in the work.
passages.ot:
Abraham's welcome of strangers is the great Old Testament picture of hospitality. He “ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them and bowed low to the ground” (Genesis 18:2), and he fed them before he knew who they were.

The law commanded love for strangers: “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).

And Israel was taught to care for those who served God and had no land of their own: “And do not neglect the Levite within your gates, since he has no portion or inheritance among you” (Deuteronomy 14:27).
passages.asks: Ask who the strangers are in your church or town whose work for Christ you could support. Ask what it would mean to send someone on their way ‘in a manner worthy of God’. And ask whether you think of your home, your table and your money as part of the mission.

passages.t: Diotrephes, who loves to be first
passages.happening:
“I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction” (verse 9).

“So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Now the trouble. The elder had written to the church, perhaps a letter now lost; some think it was 2 John. Diotrephes would not accept it.

His name is Greek and means ‘nourished by Zeus’. We do not know whether he held an office or simply ran a house church. Scholars have read the quarrel as personal ambition, as local leaders resisting a senior leader from outside, or as an early step toward the single presiding bishop found in the second century. The letter does not tell us. It tells us what he did.

And what he did is a list of a leader who treats a church as his own. He ‘loves to be first’, one Greek word found only here in the New Testament. He will not accept instruction from outside. He spreads ‘malicious slander’. He refuses to welcome the travelling workers. He forbids others to welcome them. And he puts out of the church those who try.

Notice how the elder answers. He does not slander back. He says he will come and ‘call attention’ to what Diotrephes has done, openly, face to face. He names the wrong plainly. He does not excuse it because the man holds a position. And he does not let one man define the church.
passages.ot:
Diotrephes has an ancestor in Korah, who gathered men against Moses and Aaron and said, “Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?” (Numbers 16:3). Korah accused others of the very pride that drove him.

The prophets spoke against shepherds who used the flock for themselves: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves” (Ezekiel 34:2).

And the proverb gives the warning: “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18).
passages.hard:
What should a Christian do when a church leader behaves like Diotrephes?

The elder's own answer is a pattern. He names the wrong plainly. He plans to deal with it openly, in person. He does not answer slander with slander. And he points his friend to what is good (verse 11).

Jesus taught the opposite of Diotrephes' way: “If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all” (Mark 9:35). Leaders in the church are servants, accountable to Christ and to his word.

This letter does not ask anyone to stay under a leader who controls, shames or harms them.

If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. Being taken in by someone who seemed godly is not a sign of weak faith; the Corinthians were taken in too. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. A pastor or counsellor outside that church may help you sort out what happened. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask where you want to be first, at home, at work or in church. Ask whether you have ever kept someone out to keep control. And ask how you would answer a wrong done to you without doing the same wrong back.

passages.happening:
“Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God” (verse 11).

“Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Verse 11 stands between Diotrephes and Demetrius, and it gives the point of the letter. People become like what they copy. Gaius has two examples in front of him. He is to follow the good one.

The second sentence sounds like 1 John. Those born of God show the family likeness in what they do. Doing good shows that a person ‘is of God’. Doing evil shows that he ‘has not seen God’, whatever he says.

Then Demetrius. Verse 12 reads like a short letter of recommendation, a common kind of letter in the ancient world. Demetrius probably carried this letter to Gaius. Three witnesses stand behind him: everyone who knows him, ‘the truth itself’, and the elder. His life matched what he believed, and people could see it.
passages.ot:
The call to choose the good echoes the prophets: “Seek good, not evil, so that you may live” (Amos 5:14). And the psalm: “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm 34:14).

A good name confirmed by others is the proverb's treasure: “A good name is more desirable than great riches” (Proverbs 22:1).
passages.asks: Ask whose example you are copying, and whether it is a good one. Ask whether your life backs up what you say you believe. And ask who could be helped by a word from you that vouches for them.

passages.happening:
“I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink. Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face” (verses 13-14).

“Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The ending is very like the end of 2 John. The elder has more to say, but he would rather say it in person. Writing was a second-best way to be present.

‘Peace to you.’ After a letter that names a church quarrel, the elder ends with peace.

Notice the last words. The believers are ‘friends’, and the elder asks Gaius to greet each of them ‘by name’. In a letter that has just described a leader who pushed people out, the last word is about each person being known and greeted.
passages.ot:
‘Peace to you’ carries the old greeting of Israel, shalom. The priests' blessing ended with it: “may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26).

And God knows his people by name: “I have called you by your name; you are Mine” (Isaiah 43:1).
passages.asks: Ask whom you need to see face to face instead of writing to. Ask whether the people in your church are greeted by name. And ask who would be glad to hear from you this week.
